title-group.article-title: RNF90 promotes hepatic steatosis by degrading CPT1α to suppress fatty acid oxidation

abstract.p: Hepatic fatty acid oxidation (FAO) is crucial for maintaining hepatic lipid homeostasis, and dysregulation of hepatic lipid metabolism is closely associated with metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease. However, the molecular mechanisms governing FAO in hepatocytes remain incompletely understood. Here, we demonstrate that RNF90 is essential for FAO regulation, with its expression significantly upregulated in fatty liver. Further investigation revealed that RNF90 is transcriptionally activated by KLF5 and functions as an E3 ubiquitin ligase to promote the ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal degradation of carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1α (CPT1α), a rate-limiting enzyme in mitochondrial FAO. Hepatocyte-specific RNF90 knockout significantly increased CPT1α protein expression, enhanced FAO activity, and alleviated hepatic steatosis, as evidenced by reduced hepatic lipid accumulation and triglyceride levels. Conversely, overexpression of wildtype RNF90 (but not its E3 ligase-deficient mutant) exerted the opposite effects. Function rescue experiments further confirm that CPT1α is indispensable for RNF90-mediated regulation of FAO and protection against hepatic steatosis. Collectively, our study establishes RNF90 as a critical regulator of hepatic lipid metabolism and identifies the KLF5/RNF90/CPT1α axis as a potential therapeutic target for metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease.

body.p: Metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MASLD), previously known as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), is the most common chronic liver disease that is affecting over one-third of the global population (1). It comprises a broad clinicopathological spectrum, ranging from simple steatosis (MAFL) to the more severe metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). Generally, simple steatosis is characterized by excessive triglyceride (TG) accumulation in hepatocytes, a reversible state generally considered benign. However, if left untreated, MAFL can progress sequentially to MASH, cirrhosis, and ultimately hepatocellular carcinoma (2). Dysregulation of hepatic lipid metabolism constitutes the pathogenic core of MASLD, making the management of hepatic steatosis a pivotal therapeutic target to impede disease progression. Hepatic lipid homeostasis is a tightly orchestrated process involving lipid uptake, de novo synthesis, and fatty acid oxidation (FAO), and perturbations in any of these interconnected pathways can disrupt metabolic balance, thereby precipitating hepatic steatosis (3, 4). Despite substantial research efforts, the intricate molecular networks governing hepatic lipid homeostasis remain incompletely elucidated, which contributes to the paucity of Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved therapeutic agents for MASLD. Given the disease’s high global prevalence and potentially life-threatening complications, there is an urgent imperative to delineate its underlying pathogenic mechanisms and identify novel therapeutic targets to address this unmet clinical need.

FAO is a crucial mechanism for maintaining hepatic lipid homeostasis, as it efficiently converts excess fatty acids into usable energy mainly through the mitochondrial β-oxidation pathway (4, 5). For FAO to proceed efficiently, the precise transport of fatty acids into mitochondria is indispensable; this process relies on a well-orchestrated shuttle system, with carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1α (CPT1α) acting as its core component. Specifically, CPT1α functions as a key rate-limiting enzyme that mediates the translocation of long-chain fatty acids across the mitochondrial membrane, thereby initiating their subsequent oxidation (6, 7). Accumulating evidence has underscored the tight link between CPT1α and hepatic steatosis. Reduced expression or impaired activity of CPT1α has been shown to compromise FAO efficiency, leading to the development of hepatic steatosis (8, 9). Conversely, overexpression of CPT1α can alleviate the progression of MASLD induced by a high-fat diet (HFD) (9, 10), highlighting the enzyme’s potential as a therapeutic modulator for the disease. Notably, the stability and enzymatic activity of CPT1α are finely regulated by posttranslational modifications, such as ubiquitination, phosphorylation, and acetylation (11, 12, 13). Given the centrality of CPT1α in regulating FAO and its clear association with MASLD pathogenesis, further exploration of the regulatory mechanisms governing CPT1α expression or activity represents a promising therapeutic strategy for the prevention and treatment of MASLD.

RNF90, initially identified as glycogenin-interacting protein (also designated TRIM7/GNIP), was implicated in the regulation of glycogen metabolism (14, 15). As a member of RING-type E3 ubiquitin ligases family, RNF90 possesses a conserved RBCC motif (RING finger, B-box, coiled-coil domain) and a C-terminal PRY-SPRY domain, which are critical structural features enabling it to mediate the ubiquitin modification of specific substrates. Emerging evidences have indicated that RNF90 exerts vital regulatory effects across multiple biological processes, including metabolism, immune response, and ferroptosis through the modification of its specific substrates (14, 16, 17). Furthermore, aberrant RNF90 expression has been shown involved in several pathophysiological processes, such as virus infection, tumorigenesis, and metastasis (18, 19, 20). Notably, our previous RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) analysis of liver tissues from mice with a hepatic steatosis phenotype revealed a dramatic upregulation of RNF90 mRNA expression. However, the regulatory mechanisms governing RNF90 expression and the underlying molecular pathways through which RNF90 participates in hepatic steatosis remain poorly understood.

In this study, we identified that the transcription factor KLF5 directly binds to the RNF90 promoter region to enhance RNF90 expression in MASLD samples. In vitro and in vivo functional experiments demonstrated that RNF90 overexpression impairs FAO and exacerbates hepatic steatosis, whereas RNF90 deficiency shows opposite effects. Mechanistically, we uncovered that RNF90 interacts with CPT1α and catalyzes the K48-linked ubiquitination-dependent degradation, thereby reducing CPT1α protein stability and ultimately inhibiting FAO activity. Notably, restoring CPT1α expression in hepatocytes with RNF90 overexpression effectively abrogated the inhibitory effect of RNF90 on FAO. Taken together, our study identifies a novel KLF5/RNF90/CPT1α regulatory axis as a potential therapeutic target for the treatment of MASLD.

sec.title: KLF5 mediates RNF90 expression upregulation in the liver of hepatic steatosis
sec.p:
To determine whether RNF90 is involved in hepatic lipid metabolism, we established MAFL mouse models and a serious MASH mouse model. H&E and Oil red O staining of liver sections revealed a marked increase in lipid accumulation (Fig. 1A), confirming the successful induction of hepatic steatosis in these models. Next, we examined RNF90 expression in liver tissues from these mouse models, and found that RNF90 levels were significantly elevated at both the mRNA and protein levels (Fig. 1, B–D). We further assessed RNF90 expression in hepatocyte cell lines (HepG2 and AML12) treated with POA (a mixture of palmitic acid and oleic acid). Quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR) and western blot analyses showed that RNF90 expression increased in a time-dependent manner at both the mRNA and protein levels (Fig. 1, E–H). Collectively, these results demonstrate that RNF90 expression is upregulated during MASLD development. To elucidate the molecular mechanism underlying RNF90 upregulation in MASLD, we first sought to identify transcription factors that potentially regulate RNF90 expression. We analyzed the promoter sequences of the human and mouse RNF90 genes using FIMOs (Find Individual Motif Occurrences), GTRD (Gene Transcription Regulation Database) and ChIP_Atlas database. This cross-species analysis results revealed that KLF5 was among the top-scoring candidates transcription factor, and further sequence inspection indicated three potential KLF5 binding sites within the RNF90 promoter (Fig. 1, I and J). Subsequently, we investigated the correlation between KLF5 and RNF90 expression. Overexpression of KLF5 increased RNF90 mRNA and protein levels in a dose-dependent manner, whereas silencing of KLF5 decreased RNF90 expression (Fig. 1, K and L). Consistent with this, KLF5 protein expression was also significantly increased in steatotic liver tissues and in POA-treated hepatocytes (Figs. 1, B and C, S1, F–H), confirming a positive correlation between KLF5 and RNF90 expression. To verify whether KLF5 directly regulates RNF90 transcription, we cloned the RNF90 promoter sequence into the pGL3-basic vector and performed dual-luciferase reporter assays to evaluate the effect of KLF5 on RNF90 promoter activity. Overexpression of KLF5 enhanced RNF90 promoter activity in a dose-dependent manner, while KLF5 knockdown dramatically reduced this activity (Fig. 1M). To map the KLF5-responsive regions within the RNF90 promoter, we constructed a series of RNF90 promoter deletion mutants. Dual-luciferase assays showed that deletion of one or two potential KLF5 binding sites significantly reduced KLF5-induced promoter activation, and deletion of all three sites almost completely abrogated this positive regulatory effect (Fig. 1N). Finally, chromatin immunoprecipitation PCR (ChIP-PCR) demonstrated a significant enrichment of KLF5 at the predicted binding sites within the RNF90 promoter region (Fig. 1O), confirming that KLF5 directly binds to these sites to regulate RNF90 promoter activity. Taken together, these findings indicate that RNF90 expression is upregulated during hepatic steatosis development and is positively regulated by KLF5.Figure 1

sec.title: RNF90 aggravates hepatic steatosis in vitro
sec.p:
To investigate the role of RNF90 in hepatic lipid metabolism, we generated stable RNF90-knockdown cell lines in HepG2 cells using lentiviruses encoding shRNA targeting RNF90 (shRNF90). The efficiency of RNF90 knockdown was validated at both the mRNA and protein levels (Figs. 2A and S1A). Given that the shRNF90-2# and shRNF90-3# cell lines exhibited more profound silencing efficiency, these two stable cell lines were selected for subsequent experiments. Scramble control and RNF90-knockdown HepG2 cells were treated with POA for 24 h to establish a fatty liver cell model. Oil red O staining showed that RNF90 knockdown significantly ameliorated POA-induced hepatic lipid accumulation in HepG2 cells, whereas silencing RNF90 had no marked effect on lipid accumulation under basal conditions (Figs. 2B and S1B). Moreover, RNF90 deficiency markedly reduced POA-induced intracellular TG levels (Fig. 2C). Consistently, knockdown of RNF90 in AML12 cells also reduced intracellular lipid accumulation (Figs. 2, D–G and S1, C–D). Furthermore, we constructed stable cell lines overexpressing wild-type RNF90 (RNF90-WT) and its E3 ligase-deficient mutant (C29A; C32A, and RNF90-DM) in HepG2 and AML12 cells, with overexpression efficiency confirmed at the mRNA and protein levels (Figs. 2, H and I and S1E). Oil red O staining and TG analysis showed that lipid deposition was significantly exacerbated in POA-treated RNF90-overexpressing hepatocytes, whereas overexpression of RNF90-DM did not affect hepatic steatosis compared to the control group (Figs. 2, J and K and S1F). Altogether, these findings demonstrate that RNF90 promotes hepatic lipid accumulation depending on its E3 ligase activity.Figure 2

sec.title: RNF90 interacts with CPT1α and promotes its K48-linked ubiquitination
sec.p:
To identify key regulators of RNF90-mediated hepatic steatosis, we performed RNF90-targeted co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) coupled with affinity mass spectrometry analysis in L02 cells stably overexpressing RNF90 (Fig. S1G). By filtering peptide spectra based on protein score and integrating functional annotation, CPT1α was identified as a potential interacting partner of RNF90 (Fig. 3A). To confirm the association between RNF90 and CPT1α, we first examined their subcellular localization. Confocal microscopy revealed significant colocalization of the two proteins (Fig. 3, B and C), supporting a possible physical interaction. This hypothesis was further validated by reciprocal co-IP assays, which demonstrated that both exogenous and endogenous RNF90 bound to CPT1α, and vice versa (Fig. 3, D and E). Given that RNF90 belongs to the RING-type E3 ligase family, we conducted ubiquitination assays to determine whether RNF90 mediates CPT1α ubiquitination. Compared to cells expressing hemagglutinin (HA)-CPT1α and myc-Ub alone, overexpression of RNF90-WT markedly increased CPT1α ubiquitination. In contrast, RNF90-DM had minimal effects on CPT1α ubiquitination (Figs. 3F and S1H). Consistently, knockdown RNF90 dramatically reduced the ubiquitination level of CPT1α (Figs. 3G and S1I). To elucidate the type of polyubiquitin chains involved, we employed plasmids encoding ubiquitin mutants at the K48 and K63 sites—the two most common types of polyubiquitination. Our results showed that RNF90 significantly enhanced K48-linked polyubiquitination of CPT1α (Figs. 3, H and I and S1, J–K). Using ubiquitination prediction tools and referencing previous studies, we selected three potential ubiquitination sites (Lys195, Lys292, and Lys772 residues) on CPT1α. Site-directed mutagenesis of these residues (K195R, K292R, and K772R) revealed that the K195R mutation in CPT1α strongly impaired RNF90-induced polyubiquitination, whereas the K292R and K772R mutations had no significant impact (Figs. 3J and S1L). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that RNF90 physically interacts with CPT1α and mediates its K48-linked polyubiquitination at lysine 195.Figure 3

B, representative immunofluorescence staining images showing the subcellular localization of RNF90 and CPT1α protein in L02 cells. C, quantitative analysis of the colocalization between RNF90 and CPT1α in the indicated regions from panel B. D–E, co-IP analysis to detect the interaction between RNF90 and CPT1α proteins using exogenous-specific antibodies (D) and endogenous-specific antibodies (E) in HEK293T cells. F–G, measurement of CPT1α ubiquitination levels in HEK293T cells cotransfected with Myc-Ub, HA-CPT1α, and either Flag-tagged RNF90 wildtype or its E3 ligase deficiency mutant plasmids (F) or with Myc-Ub, HA-CPT1α, and RNF90 knockdown plasmids (G). H–I, analysis of the ubiquitination type of CPT1α catalyzed by RNF90 in HEK293T cells cotransfected with HA- CPT1α, Flag-RNF90, and the indicated Myc-Ub-K48 mutants (H) or Myc-Ub-K63 mutants (I). sec.title: RNF90 regulates CPT1α stability in an E3 ligase activity-dependent manner
sec.p:
Given that K48-linked ubiquitin chains are the most prevalent proteasome-targeting signal (21, 22), we investigated whether RNF90 regulates CPT1α protein stability. Overexpression of RNF90-WT induced a dose-dependent reduction in CPT1α protein levels, whereas RNF90-DM failed to exert a similar effect (Figs. 4A and S1M). To mechanistically define this regulatory effect, we performed protein half-life assays in 293T cells cotransfected with HA-CPT1α alone or in combination with RNF90-WT or RNF90-DM. After transfection, cells were treated with the protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX) at different time points. Western blot analysis revealed that RNF90-WT significantly shortened the half-life of CPT1α, while RNF90-DM had no such effect (Fig. 4, B–D). Notably, overexpression of RNF90-WT neither reduced the protein level of the CPT1α-K195R mutant in a dose-dependent manner nor altered its half-life (Figs. 4, E–G and S1N), indicating that CPT1α stability depends on RNF90-mediated ubiquitination. In contrast, knockdown of RNF90 prolonged CPT1α protein stability (Fig. 4, H and I), further supporting the specificity of this regulatory axis. Subsequently, we explored the degradation pathway underlying RNF90-mediated CPT1α reduction by treating cells with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 or the lysosome inhibitors chloroquine or NH4Cl. As shown in Figure 4J, RNF90-mediated CPT1α degradation was abrogated by MG132 treatment but not by lysosome inhibitors, demonstrating that RNF90 promotes CPT1α turnover via the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (Fig. 4J). To validate whether RNF90 regulates CPT1α expression in the context of hepatic steatosis, we examined CPT1α protein levels in POA-treated hepatocytes. Consistently, overexpression of RNF90-WT but not RNF90-DM reduced CPT1α protein levels, while RNF90 knockdown significantly increased CPT1α expression (Figs. 4K and S1O). Corresponding to changes in CPT1α levels (a key rate-limiting enzyme for FAO), FAO activity was attenuated in POA-treated HepG2 cells overexpressing WT RNF90 (but not RNF90-DM), whereas RNF90 deficiency resulted in enhanced FAO activity (Fig. 4L). Altogether, these results demonstrate that RNF90 destabilizes CPT1α in an E3 ligase activity-dependent manner, and this regulatory mechanism is conserved in the setting of hepatic steatosis.Figure 4

sec.title: Hepatic RNF90 deficiency alleviates diet-induced hepatic steatosis in mice by enhancing FAO
sec.p:
To investigate the effects of RNF90 on FAO and hepatic lipid metabolism in vivo, we generated hepatocyte-specific Rnf90 knockout (RNF90-HKO) mice by crossing albumin-Cre transgenic mice with Rnf90flox/flox (RNF90-Flox) mice (Fig. S1, P–Q). Western blot analysis confirmed a significant reduction in hepatic RNF90 protein expression in RNF90-HKO mice compared to littermate RNF90-Flox controls (Fig. S1R). RNF90-HKO mice and their littermate RNF90-Flox were then randomly assigned to either a HFD or normal chow diet (NCD) for 14 weeks. Under HFD feeding, both genotypes exhibited increased body weight, liver weight, and liver-to-body weight ratio (LW/BW) compared to those on NCD. Notably, RNF90-HKO mice showed attenuated increases in these parameters compared to controls under HFD conditions, whereas no genotype-dependent differences were observed in mice fed NCD (Fig. 5, A–C). Histological analysis via H&E and Oil Red O staining revealed significantly reduced hepatic lipid accumulation in RNF90-HKO mice compared to controls after 14 weeks of HFD feeding, whereas lipid deposition was comparable between genotypes under NCD (Fig. 5, D and E). Consistently, biochemical analysis demonstrated that hepatic TG and total cholesterol (TC) contents were dramatically lower in HFD-fed RNF90-HKO mice than in HFD-fed controls (Fig. 5F). To confirm the reproducibility of these findings, we established an additional MASLD model using a high-fat, high fructose and high-cholesterol (HFHC) diet for 19 weeks, and observed a similar protective effect of RNF90 deficiency on hepatic lipid accumulation (Fig. 5, G–J). Next, we sought to elucidate whether RNF90 knockout alleviates hepatic steatosis by enhancing hepatic FAO in vivo. We first examined the expression of CPT1α and found a marked upregulation of CPT1α protein in the livers of RNF90-HKO mice fed either HFD or HFHC compared to their respective controls (Figs. 5K and S1S). Consistent with this increase in CPT1α, FAO activity was significantly enhanced in hepatic tissues of RNF90-HKO mice under both dietary stress conditions (Fig. 5L). In addition, given that FAO generates acetyl-CoA for ketogenesis or entry into the tricarboxylic acid cycle, we measured mitochondrial hydroxyl methyl glutaryl-CoA synthase 2 (HMGCS2), a rate-limiting enzyme in ketone body production. RT-qPCR analysis showed increased HMGCS2 mRNA levels in RNF90-HKO livers under dietary stress (Fig. 5M). Furthermore, RNF90 deficiency led to elevated levels of β-hydroxybutyric acid and ATP, metabolic indicators of enhanced fatty acid β-oxidation (Fig. 5, N–O). Collectively, these in vivo findings demonstrate that hepatocyte-specific RNF90 deficiency promotes hepatic FAO and thereby ameliorates diet-induced hepatic steatosis across two distinct MASLD models.Figure 5

sec.title: Hepatic RNF90 overexpression suppresses FAO and exacerbates hepatic lipid accumulation
sec.p:
To further confirm the role of RNF90 in FAO and hepatic steatosis, we generated hepatocyte-specific RNF90-overexpressing mouse models through tail vein injection of AAV serotype 8 (AAV8) vectors encoding wild-type RNF90 (AAV8-RNF90-WT) or its E3 ligase-deficient mutant (AAV8-RNF90-DM) into mice fed a HFD or HFHC (Fig. S1T). For tracking viral expression, the AAV8 vector co-expressed enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP), so AAV8-EGFP served as the control group. Mice were sacrificed 10 weeks after AAV8 injection for pathological analysis. Small animal imaging confirmed the preferential accumulation of the injected adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors in the liver (Fig. 6A), and immunoblotting analysis revealed significantly upregulated RNF90 protein expression in liver tissues from both AAV8-RNF90-WT and AAV8-RNF90-DM groups compared to the control group (Fig. 6, B and C). Notably, overexpression of RNF90-WT dramatically reduced CPT1α protein levels, whereas the RNF90-DM mutant had no such effect (Fig. 6, B and C). Under both HFD and HFHC conditions, wildtype RNF90 overexpression markedly exacerbated hepatic lipid deposition and increased TG and TC levels (Fig. 6, D–F). Furthermore, AAV8-RNF90-WT-infected mice exhibited impaired hepatic FAO, as evidenced by reduced FAO activity, downregulated HMGCS2 mRNA expression, and decreased levels of β-hydroxybutyrate and ATP (Fig. 6, G–J). In contrast, overexpression of RNF90-DM showed no significant differences from the control group. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that RNF90 suppresses FAO and promotes hepatic lipid accumulation in a manner dependent on its E3 ligase activity.Figure 6

B–C, immunoblotting (B) and densitometric quantification (C) of RNF90, CPT1α protein expression in liver tissues from HFD- or HFHC-fed mice injected with AAV8. β-actin was used as control, and relative protein levels were quantified by normalizing target band intensities to β-actin using Image J software (n = 4). D–E, representative images of H&E staining and Oil red O staining (D), and quantitative analysis of Oil red O-stained positive area (E) in liver tissues from AAV8-injected mice fed a HFD (14 weeks) or HFHC (19 weeks) (n = 5). F–G, measurements of liver TG, TC contents (F), and FAO activity (G) in AAV8-injected mice fed a HFD (14 weeks) or HFHC (19 weeks) (n = 8). H, RT-qPCR analysis of HMGCS2 mRNA expression in liver tissues from HFD- or HFHC-fed mice injected with AAV8. I–J, measurement of liver β-HB (I) and ATP (J) contents in AAV8-injected mice fed a HFD (14 weeks) or HFHC (19 weeks) (n = 8). sec.title: CPT1α is essential for RNF90-mediated regulation of FAO and steatosis in hepatocytes
sec.p:
To investigate the requirement of CPT1α for RNF90-mediated FAO and hepatic steatosis in hepatocytes, we performed gain-of-function and loss-of-function rescue experiments. In HepG2 cells stably overexpressing RNF90, we further transfected a CPT1α overexpression plasmid and induced a fatty liver phenotype by treating the cells with POA for 24 h (Fig. 7A). Quantification of FAO activity demonstrated that CPT1α overexpression rescued the RNF90-induced inhibition of FAO (Fig. 7B). Correspondingly, CPT1α overexpression abolished the increased lipid accumulation (Oil Red O staining) and TG content in RNF90-overexpressing cells (Fig. 7, C and D). Conversely, silencing CPT1α in RNF90-knockdown cells suppressed FAO activity and eliminated the protective effects against lipid deposition and TG accumulation mediated by RNF90 downregulation (Figs. 7, E–H and S1U). Taken together, these results confirm that CPT1α is indispensable for RNF90 to regulate FAO and prevent hepatic steatosis.Figure 7
CPT1α is essential for RNF90-mediated regulation of FAO and steatosis in hepatocytes. A, HepG2 cells stably overexpressing Flag-tagged RNF90 were transfected with either HA-tagged CPT1α plasmid or empty control plasmid. At 12 h post transfection, cells were treated with POA for 24 h, then harvested for immunoblotting analysis of Flag-tagged RNF90 and HA-tagged CPT1α protein expression, with β-actin as the loading control. B, measurement of FAO activity in HepG2 cells treated as described in (A) (n = 4). C–D, representative Oil red O staining images, quantitative analysis of Oil red O-positive area (C), and TG content quantification (D) in HepG2 cells treated as described in (A) (n = 4). E, HepG2-shRNF90-3# cells were transfected with shCPT1α plasmid or empty control plasmid. After 12 h of transfection, cells were treated with POA for 24 h, then harvested for immunoblotting analysis of RNF90 and CPT1α protein expression, with β-actin as the loading control. F, measurement of FAO activity in HepG2 cells treated as described in (E) (n = 4). G–H, representative Oil red O staining images, quantitative analysis of Oil red O-positive area (G) and TG content quantification (H) in HepG2 cells treated as described in (E) (n = 4). I, schematic diagram illustrating the underlying molecular mechanism by which the KLF5/RNF90/CPT1α axis promotes hepatic steatosis by suppressing fatty acid oxidation. Data are presented as the mean ± SD, and statistical significance was analyzed by one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test (B–D, F–H). The exact p values are indicated in each graph. CPT1α, carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1α; FAO, fatty acid oxidation; KLF5, Kruppel-like factor 5; POA, a mixture of palmitic acid and oleic acid; shRNF90, shRNA targeting RNF90; TG, triglyceride

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: MASLD has emerged as a global health crisis, primarily due to its high prevalence and the risk of progression to liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (23). This condition, characterized by abnormal lipid accumulation within hepatocytes, is intricately intertwined with dysregulation of lipid metabolism (24, 25, 26). Previous studies have demonstrated that pharmacological interventions or genetic manipulations restoring impaired hepatic FAO can effectively mitigate MASLD progression (27). Therefore, enhancing FAO to reduce excessive lipid deposition provides a promising therapeutic strategy for MASLD treatment. However, the molecular mechanisms governing hepatic FAO remain incompletely elucidated, highlighting the need for further mechanistic investigations.

FAO predominantly occurs in mitochondria and is finely regulated at multiple levels to maintain energy homeostasis. The FAO pathway is a multistep process coordinated by a series of transcription factors and key enzymes (28, 29). Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα), a core transcription factor of lipid metabolism, directly regulates the expression of key FAO-related enzymes, including CPT1α, ACOX1, and ACSL1 (30). Accumulating evidence indicates that hepatic PPARα mRNA levels are significantly downregulated in MASLD samples relative to healthy controls, and this reduction correlates with decreased CPT1α expression (31). Pharmacological activation of PPARα or enhancement of its protein stability has been shown to restore FAO and alleviate hepatic steatosis (32). As the rate-limiting enzyme of FAO, CPT1α plays a crucial role in initiating β-oxidation by catalyzing the translocation of long-chain fatty acids across the mitochondrial membrane to generate acetyl-CoA. (33). Notably, when FAO is enhanced, the consequent accumulation of acetyl-CoA not only serves as the primary substrate for ketogenesis but also induces the expression of HMGCS2, a rate-limiting enzyme of ketogenesis. Conversely, suppression of FAO reduces acetyl-CoA, thereby limiting HMGCS2-mediated ketogenesis. It is worth noting that the activity of two core FAO regulators, PPARα and CPT1α, is tightly fine-tuned via posttranslational modifications, transcriptional regulation, and protein-protein interaction networks (11, 32). RNF90, a member of the RING-type E3 ligase family, participates in diverse physiological and pathological processes, and exhibits functional complexity and heterogeneity (34). In the present study, we observed that RNF90 expression is abnormally elevated in the liver tissues of MASLD samples. Mechanistically, we demonstrated a physical interaction between RNF90 and CPT1α, and RNF90 specifically catalyzes K48-linked polyubiquitination of CPT1α at the K195 residue, thereby targeting CPT1α for proteasomal degradation and resulting in a marked reduction in CPT1α protein levels. Although this regulatory mechanism has been identified, further investigations are required to precisely map the specific domains within RNF90 and CPT1α that mediate their interaction. Our in vivo and in vitro experiments further validated the functional significance of the RNF90-CPT1α axis. Hepatocyte-specific deletion of RNF90 resulted in a significant upregulation of CPT1α protein expression in the liver, enhancement of FAO, and reduction of hepatic steatosis. In contrast, overexpression of RNF90 WT but not its E3 ligase deficiency mutant markedly reduced CPT1α protein levels, impaired FAO, and triggered severe lipid accumulation (Figs. 5 and 6). These findings highlight the critical role of RNF90-mediated CPT1α degradation in suppressing FAO under pathological conditions associated with MASLD. Rescue experiments in hepatocytes where restoration of CPT1α expression reversed the effects of RNF90 dysregulation, further confirmed a causal relationship between these two proteins in the regulation of FAO and hepatic steatosis. However, a major limitation of the current study is the lack of in vivo rescue validation in mice models and analysis of clinical samples, both of which are essential to bridge preclinical findings with human disease. In addition, we noted that alterations in RNF90 expression correlated with changes in HMGCS2 mRNA levels. This effect may be an indirect consequence of RNF90-mediated CPT1α degradation and subsequent suppression of FAO. Nevertheless, we cannot exclude the possibility that RNF90 exerts a more direct regulatory role in HMGCS2 gene transcription, for instance, by targeting a transcriptional regulator of HMGCS2 for ubiquitination and subsequent degradation or functional modification. This hypothesis will be experimentally addressed in our future studies.

Kruppel-like factors (KLFs), a family of zinc-finger transcription factors, are known to play diverse roles in the pathophysiology of metabolic-related diseases, including obesity, MASLD, and diabetes (35, 36). For instance, increased hepatic expression of KLF2 and KLF10 has been shown to promote the development of MASLD (37, 38). In addition, KLF5 has been associated with various types of cardiovascular complications and the regulation of hepatic lipid metabolism (39). In the context of our study, we found that KLF5 expression is significantly upregulated in the liver tissues of MASLD samples. Notably, there are three potential KLF5 binding sites in the proximal promoter of RNF90, and we confirmed that KLF5 can directly bind to this region and positively regulate RNF90 expression. This suggests that KLF5 mediates RNF90 upregulation during the development of MASLD, further expanding the regulatory network of lipid metabolism in MASLD. However, it is important to acknowledge that KLF5-mediated transcriptional regulation may not be the sole mechanism driving RNF90 upregulation in MASLD. Epigenetic modifications, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, and noncoding RNA (ncRNA), are well-documented to dynamically control gene expression in metabolic diseases (40, 41). Whether the dysregulation of RNF90 in MASLD involves epigenetic mechanisms remains incompletely understood. Future studies are needed to elucidate the epigenetic regulation of RNF90, which would provide a more comprehensive understanding of its dysregulation in MASLD and identify additional therapeutic targets.

In conclusion, our study establishes RNF90 as a critical regulator of hepatic FAO and uncovers a novel KLF5/RNF90/CPT1α axis in the pathogenesis of MASLD. This discovery reveals an unrecognized layer of posttranslational control in FAO, highlighting the intricate interplay among transcription factors, E3 ubiquitin ligases, and metabolic enzymes in maintaining hepatic lipid homeostasis. These findings not only deepen our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying lipid dysregulation in MASLD but also provide potential therapeutic targets for the development of innovative treatment strategies for this widespread liver disease. Future research could focus on exploring the clinical translation of these findings and further elucidating the complex regulatory network involved in MASLD pathogenesis.

sec.title: Animal experiments
sec.p: Male C57BL/6J ob/ob mice used in this study were obtained from Jinan Pengyue Laboratory Animal Breeding Co, LTD. All mice were housed under a 12-h light/dark cycle at a constant temperature (22 °C–24 °C) and humidity (50 ± 5%) in a pathogen-free environment. They had free access to food and water. Following a 1-week acclimatization period to the new environment, mice were randomly assigned to experimental groups. Mice were fed either a HFD (fat 60%, XTM04, Xietong Bio-engineering) for 12 weeks to establish MAFL model or HFHC (fat 40%, fructose 20%, cholesterol 2%, XTM05, Xietong Bio-engineering) for 19 weeks to establish MASH mouse model. Control mice were fed with NCD (fat 11.1%, XT101WC, Xietong Bio-engineering). Body weights and food intake were recorded weekly throughout the experimental period. At the end of the experiments, mice were sacrificed for collecting tissues. All animal experimental protocols were approved by the Ethical Review Committee on Laboratory Animal Research of Jiangsu Normal University (JSNU-IACUC-2024016). All mice received human care in accordance with the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals issued by the National Institutes of Health.

sec.title: Construction of hepatocytes-specific Rnf90 knockout mice
sec.p: Hepatocyte-specific Rnf90 knockout (RNF90-HKO) mice were generated by crossing Rnf90-flox/flox mice with Albumin-Cre transgenic mice. The Rnf90-flox/flox mice were constructed by Cyagen using the Cre-LoxP recombination system. Briefly, exon 4 to 6 of the Rnf90 allele were flanked by loxp sites. Four independent guide RNAs (gRNAs) targeting introns 3 and 6 of Rnf90 were designed, and a targeting vector containing these loxP-flanked exons 4 to 6 of the murine Rnf90 gene, along with two homology arms, was constructed. The targeting vector and gRNA were injected into embryonic stem cell. Positive chimeric mice were bred with C57BL/6J mice to generate Rnf90-flox heterozygous. Then, Rnf90-flox heterozygous mice cross to generate Rnf90-flox homozygous. Progeny were screened for germline transmission of the targeted alleles via PCR and sequencing. The primers used for genotyping Rnf90-HKO mice are listed in Table S1.

sec.title: Mouse AAV injection
sec.p: To specifically overexpress Rnf90 in mouse livers, we utilized the AAV8 system driven by the thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) promoter. Both RNF90 WT and its E3 ligase-deficient mutant (C29A; C32A, designated as RNF90-DM), each tagged with a Flag epitope, were separately cloned into AAV8-EGFP vectors by OBiO Technology. These purified viruses were administered to mice fed with a HFD for 4 weeks or a HFHC for 9 weeks via tail vein injection (150 μl of vector solution containing 3 × 1011 viral genomes per mouse). An equal dose of the empty AAV8-EGFP vector was used as the control. Ten weeks after viral injection, the mice were euthanized to collect liver tissues, and viral enrichment in the livers was assessed using a small animal imaging system.

sec.title: H&E staining
sec.p: The collected liver tissues were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde solution (BL539A, biosharp), embedded in paraffin, and sectioned into 3 μm thick slices. H&E staining was performed following the instructions of the hematoxylin and eosin reagent (Servicebio). Briefly, the sections were dewaxed with xylene and rehydrated through a graded ethanol series. They were then stained with hematoxylin for 5 min, differentiated with hydrochloric acid-ethanol for 1 to 3 s, and rinsed with tap water for 15 min. After counterstaining with eosin for 1 min, the sections were rinsed with distilled water. Following dehydration through a graded ethanol series, the slides were cleared in xylene three times (2 min each) to render the tissue transparent, and coverslips were carefully mounted.

sec.title: Oil red O staining
sec.p: For liver tissues staining, liver tissues embedded in Optimal Cutting Temperature compound (OCT) were cut into 3 μm-thick frozen sections, which were then treated with 60% isopropyl alcohol for 10 min. The frozen liver sections were stained with Oil Red O working solution, followed by rinsing with 60% isopropyl alcohol until the background was pale and the lipid droplets were clearly visible as red. Slides were immersed in hematoxylin solution to counterstain nuclei, and then thoroughly washed with tap water. For cellular staining, we followed the methods as previously described (42). Briefly, after fixation with 3.7% formaldehyde and permeabilization with 60% isopropyl alcohol, cells on slides were stained with freshly prepared Oil Red O working solution at room temperature. After staining, cells were rinsed with 60% isopropanol for less than 5 s, washed multiple times with PBS, and counterstained with hematoxylin prior to microscopic examination. Stained lipid droplets were observed and imaged using a microscope.

sec.title: Biochemical analysis
sec.p: The content of Triglyceride (TG) (#A110–1, Nanjing Jiancheng), TC (#A111–1, Nanjing Jiancheng), ATP (#A095–1, Nanjing Jiancheng), and β-Hydroxybutyrate (#E-BC-K785-M, Elabscience) in liver tissues or hepatocytes were measured using commercial kits following the manufacturers’ instructions. The activity of FAO was determined using the FAO assay kit (E-BC-K784-M, Elabscience) according to the protocol provided by the manufacturers.

sec.title: Plasmid construction
sec.p: The full-length coding sequences of the indicated genes in this study were obtained by PCR amplification from human complementary DNA (cDNA). Fragments of RNF90 were cloned into Flag-tagged lentiviral vectors (phage vector). The sequence of the RNF90 E3 ligase-deficient mutant (C29A, C32A) was generated using overlap PCR and subsequently cloned into the phage vector. To knock down RNF90 expression, three independent pairs of short hairpin RNA oligonucleotides targeting RNF90 (shRNF90–1#, 2#, 3#) were synthesized. After annealing, the resulting dsDNA was inserted into the pLKO1 vector, respectively. Fragments of CPT1α and KLF5 were separately inserted into HA-tagged pCAGGS vectors or Flag-tagged pCMV-3tag-8 vectors. The promoter sequences of RNF90 were amplified by PCR using genomic DNA as templates and the amplified fragments were subsequently cloned into pGL3-basic vectors (designated as pGL3-RNF90-Pro). For the generation of RNF90 promoter deletion mutants, pGL3-RNF90-Pro was used as the template, and amplification was performed via standard PCR or overlap PCR methods. All constructed plasmids were validated by DNA sequencing.

sec.title: Cell culture and treatments
sec.p: HEK293T and HepG2 cell lines were obtained from ATCC, and AML12 were kindly provided by Professor Han Yan (Zhejiang University). Cell line authenticity was confirmed by short tandem repeat profiling, and no mycoplasma contamination was detected. All cells were cultured in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM) containing 10% fetal bovine serum and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Gibco BRL) in a cell incubator at 37 °C with 5% CO2. Plasmids transfection was performed using transfection reagent according to the manufacturer’s instructions when cell confluency reached approximately 80%. For measurement of protein half-life, the corresponding plasmids were transfected into HEK293T cells as designed. At 24 h post transfection, 50 μg/ml cycloheximide (CHX, #239764, Sigma-Aldrich) was added to the cells for the indicated time periods. To identify the protein degradation pathway, cells were pretreated separately with 15 μM proteasome inhibitor MG132, lysosome inhibitor 100 μM chloroquine or 20 μM NH4Cl for 1 h prior to CHX treatment. For induction of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease cell models, HepG2 or AML12 cells were treated with a 1 mM free fatty acid mixture (Palmitic acid: Oleic acid = 1:2) for the indicated time periods. The FFA mixture was prepared as previously described (42). Briefly, 50 mM stock solutions of palmitic acid (Sigma-Aldrich) and oleic acid were separately prepared in 50% ethanol and sterile-filtered through a 0.22 μm membrane. A palmitic acid:oleic acid mixture (1:2) was combined with DMEM containing 1% fatty acid-free bovine serum albumin (BSA) to generate a 1 mM POA-BSA working solution. Control cells were treated with DMEM supplemented with 1% fatty acid-free BSA and 0.5% ethanol.

sec.title: Immunofluorescence staining
sec.p: Cells were seeded on glass coverslips in 24-well plates and cultured until reaching 50 to 60% confluence. After co-transfection with Flag-RNF90 and HA-CPT1α plasmids, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde and permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100. Following blocking with 5% BSA for 1 h at room temperature, cells were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against Flag and HA diluted in 1% BSA/PBS. After three washes with PBS, cells were incubated with Alexa Fluor 488- and Alexa Fluor 594-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature in the dark. Coverslips were mounted onto glass slides using antifade mounting medium containing 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) and visualized under a confocal laser scanning microscope (TCS SP8; Leica). Image analysis was performed using ImageJ software, and the colocalization coefficient was calculated using the Pearson’s correlation method.

sec.title: Promoter activity measurement assay
sec.p: Promoter activity was evaluated using a dual-luciferase reporter assay system. Briefly, HEK293T or HepG2 cells were seeded in 24-well plates and cotransfected with the pGL3-RNF90-Pro plasmid, pRL-TK plasmid (as an internal control), and the indicated effector plasmids. At 30 h post transfection, cells were lysed with passive lysis buffer (Promega), and luciferase activities were measured using the Dual-Luciferase Reporter Assay Kit (Promega) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Results are presented as relative promoter activity, calculated by normalizing firefly luciferase luminescence to Renilla luciferase luminescence.

sec.title: Construction of RNF90 overexpression and knockdown stable cell lines
sec.p: Stable hepatocyte lines overexpressing or knocked down for RNF90 were generated using a lentiviral system as previously described (26). The Flag-tagged RNF90 lentiviral vector or lentiviral vectors harboring shRNF90 (shRNF90–1#, 2#, 3#) (as described above) and their respective control vectors were cotransfected into HEK293T cells with packaging plasmids (pSPAX2 and pMD2.G). Viral supernatants were collected at 48 and 72 h post transfection, filtered through a 0.45 μm filter, and used to infect target cells (HepG2 or AML12) in the presence of polybrene. At 24 h after infection, cells were selected with 2 μg/ml puromycin for 7 to 10 days to obtain stable clones. The efficiency of overexpression or knockdown was evaluated by RT-qPCR and western blotting.

sec.title: RNA extraction and RT-qPCR
sec.p: Total RNA was extracted from liver tissues (30 mg) or cultured cells using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen) following the manufacturer’s protocol. RNA concentration and purity were determined by measuring absorbance at 260 nm and 280 nm using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific), with an A260/A280 ratio of 1.9 to 2.1 indicating high-quality RNA. cDNA was reverse-transcribed using a kit with gDNA eraser (Vazyme-R212V21.1) according to the instructions. RT-qPCR was performed using SYBR Green Mix (DBI-2044) on a StepOne Real-Time PCR Detection System (ABI 7500). Relative mRNA expression levels of target genes were calculated using the 2−ΔΔCT method, with β-actin serving as the internal reference gene. Primer sequences used for RT-qPCR are listed in Table S1.

sec.title: ChIP assay
sec.p: HepG2 cells were cross-linked with 1% formaldehyde at room temperature for 10 min, and the reaction was quenched with glycine. Cells were harvested, washed twice with cold PBS, and lysed in lysis buffer containing protease inhibitors on ice. Nuclei were isolated and chromatin was sheared into 400 to 800 bp fragments by sonication (Scientz) on ice (5 s on/8 s off, 15 min). After centrifugation at 12,000 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C, a 5% aliquot of the supernatant was retained as input DNA. The remaining chromatin was incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against KLF5 or immunoglobulin G (IgG) (as a negative control) under rotation. Protein A/G agarose beads (GE Healthcare) were added the next day and incubated for at least 2 h at 4 °C to capture antibody-chromatin complexes. Beads were washed sequentially with wash buffers to remove nonspecific binding. Immune complexes were eluted with elution buffer containing proteinase K, and cross-links were reversed by heating at 65 °C overnight. Purified DNA was obtained using a commercial kit and analyzed by quantitative PCR with specific primers targeting the RNF90 promoter region (primer sequences listed in Table S1).

sec.title: Protein extraction and western blot
sec.p: Total proteins were extracted from liver tissues or cultured cells using radio-immunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) lysis buffer supplemented with protease/phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (APExBIO). Tissues were homogenized on ice, and cell lysates were incubated on ice for 30 min, followed by centrifugation at 12,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C. The protein supernatant was collected and quantified using a bicinchoninic acid (BCA) Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). After denaturation with SDS-loading buffer containing DTT at 95 °C for 10 min, equal amounts of protein were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes (Millipore). Following blocking with 5% skim milk in Tris-buffered saline with Tween-20 (TBST) for at least 1 h at room temperature, the membrane were incubated overnight at 4 °C with the indicated primary antibodies. After three washes with TBST, membranes were incubated with corresponding HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (Jackson) for 1 h at room temperature. Protein expression signals were detected using an ECL reagent (Millipore) and visualized with a chemiluminescence imaging system (GE Amersham Imager 600). Band intensities were quantified using ImageJ software, and relative protein levels were normalized to β-actin. The specificity validation of each antibody can be verified by researchers through the manufacturer's official website and relevant citations.

sec.title: Coimmunoprecipitation assay
sec.p: HEK293T cells were cotransfected with Flag-tagged RNF90 and HA-tagged CPT1α plasmids. At 48 h post transfection, cells were lysed in RIPA buffer containing protease inhibitor cocktail on ice for 30 min. After centrifugation, a 10% aliquot of the supernatant was retained as input, and the remaining lysate were incubated with anti-Flag magnetic beads (B26102, Bimake) or anti-HA magnetic beads (B26202, Bimake) overnight at 4 °C with rotation. For endogenous co-IP, protein supernatants were prepared from collected cells as described above, then co-incubated with the indicated primary antibodies and protein A/G agarose beads (GE Healthcare) overnight at 4 °C with rotation. Corresponding IgG antibodies were used as negative controls. Beads from both exogenous and endogenous co-IP were washed six times with immunoprecipitation (IP) wash buffer, then resuspended in 2 × SDS loading buffer and boiled at 95 °C for 10 min to elute bound proteins. Immunoprecipitated proteins and input samples were analyzed by western blotting using the indicated antibodies.

sec.title: Mass spectrometry analysis
sec.p: L02 hepatocytes stably overexpressing Flag-tagged RNF90 and their control cells were subjected to co-IP. This co-IP was performed as described above, using anti-FLAG M2 magnetic beads (Sigma-Aldrich, cat. no. M8823) in IP lysis buffer. Eluted proteins from the co-IP were then analyzed by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis (BGI Co). Candidate RNF90-interacting proteins were initially filtered by two criteria: they were exclusively detected in the RNF90-overexpressing group (undetectable in the control group) and had a count of unique peptides > 2. Subsequently, to identify substrate proteins of RNF90 that regulate FAO, further screening was conducted based on the known functional roles of the candidate proteins and evidence from relevant literature. The mass spectrometry raw data have been deposited in the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the iProX partner repository under the accession code PXD069230.

sec.title: Ubiquitination assay
sec.p: HEK293T cells were cotransfected with plasmids encoding HA-tagged CPT1α, Myc-tagged ubiquitin (Myc-Ub) and either Flag-tagged RNF90 (wild-type or E3 ligase-deficient mutant) or empty vector (as a control). At 24 h post transfection, cells were harvested and lysed in IP buffer T supplemented with protease inhibitor cocktail. Lysates were denatured by adding 1% SDS and heating at 95 °C for 10 min, then diluted 10-fold with IP buffer T. After sonication, samples were centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C. The supernatants were incubated with anti-HA magnetic beads (B26202, Bimake) overnight at 4 °C with rotation. Beads were washed six times with IP wash buffer, resuspended in 2 × SDS loading buffer, and boiled at 95 °C for 10 min. Ubiquitinated proteins were analyzed by western blotting using the indicated antibodies to detect immunoprecipitated protein levels.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The relevant experiments were performed at least three independent biological replicates, and results are presented as the mean ± SD. Statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism 9.0 software (GraphPad Software). Comparisons between two groups were analyzed using an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t test. For multiple group comparisons, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test was used. A p value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.p: All data are included within the article or Supplementary Information or available from the corresponding authors on request.
